hints: Think of what two particles must always be present in a complex, a metal centre and the species donating electron pairs to it.
walkthrough:
Picture the building blocks**
Imagine $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ sitting in front of you. In the middle you have $\text{Co}^{2+}$, and around it you have six water molecules each using a lone pair to form a dative bond to the cobalt. That whole assembly with an overall charge is the complex ion.
Final answer: A complex ion is a central metal atom or ion surrounded by and bonded to one or more ligands.

hints: Recall the characteristic test for $\text{Co}^{2+}(aq)$ with $\text{NaOH}$, think about whether $\text{OH}^{-}$ replaces water fully or forms a hydroxide solid.
For excess concentrated ammonia, think about whether $\text{NH}_3$ can act as a stronger ligand than water and stay in solution.
Remember the starting colour of $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ is pink, and consider what blue solid and blue solution products are known for cobalt(II).
Write ionic equations by balancing ligands lost as free $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ against ligands gained, keeping charge balanced.
Ask yourself if $\text{OH}^{-}$ causes a change of ligand set in solution or removal of the metal as an insoluble hydroxide.
Ask yourself if $\text{NH}_3$ in excess causes a precipitate or a soluble substitution product with all six waters replaced.
walkthrough:
Separate the two reagents in your mind**
With dilute $\text{NaOH}$ you are adding $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions. $\text{Co}^{2+}$ forms an insoluble hydroxide, so the pink $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ is removed from solution as solid blue $\text{Co(OH)}_2$. This can also be written as $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{(OH)}_2\text{]}$. The key point is you see a blue precipitate, not a blue solution.

Balance the precipitation equation**
Start with $$\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Co(OH)}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms and charge: Co 1 to 1, O 8 to 8, H 14 to 14, charge 0 to 0. No ligands remain bound except hydroxide. Because no ligand stays in the coordination sphere in solution and a solid forms, call this precipitation, also accepted as acid-base.

Switch to excess ammonia**
Concentrated $\text{NH}_3$ is a good ligand that competes with water. In excess it replaces all six waters to give the soluble hexaammine complex, so you keep a solution, which is blue: $$\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Again charge balances at $2+$ both sides. Because one ligand directly swaps for another with no change in coordination number, this is ligand exchange, also called substitution or displacement.

Final answer: With $\text{NaOH}$: blue precipitate / solid of $\text{Co(OH)}_2$.
$\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Co(OH)}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, precipitation / acid-base reaction.
With excess $\text{NH}_3$: blue solution of $\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$.
$\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, ligand exchange / substitution.

hints: Identify what $\text{Ag}^{+}$ does to free $\text{Cl}^{-}$ in solution and how that changes $\text{[Cl}^{-}\text{]}$ in the equilibrium expression.

Link the fall in $\text{[Cl}^{-}\text{]}$ to the direction the equilibrium $$\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{[CoCl}_4\text{]}^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ must shift, and recall the colours of the two cobalt species.
walkthrough:
Spot the side reaction**
Silver ions love chloride ions: $\text{Ag}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{AgCl(s)}$, a white precipitate. Adding $\text{AgNO}_3$ therefore sucks $\text{Cl}^{-}$ out of the cobalt equilibrium mixture.

Apply Le Chatelier to the cobalt equilibrium**
For $$\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{[CoCl}_4\text{]}^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ lowering $\text{[Cl}^{-}\text{]}$ means the system tries to replace it by shifting left. The blue tetrahedral $\text{[CoCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}$ converts back to pink octahedral $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$, so you see blue to pink plus white $\text{AgCl}$.

Final answer: Blue solution turns pink and white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ forms.
$\text{Ag}^{+}$ removes $\text{Cl}^{-}$, so $\text{[Cl}^{-}\text{]}$ decreases and equilibrium shifts to the left, reforming pink $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$.

hints: Picture an octahedron with Co in the centre, consider the two distinct ways three identical $\text{NH}_3$ ligands can be arranged around it.
Recall the names for the isomer with three identical ligands occupying one triangular face versus the isomer with three identical ligands around the meridian.
walkthrough:
Build the fac isomer**
Put Co in the centre of an octahedron. Choose one corner for $\text{NH}_3$, then put the other two $\text{NH}_3$ on the two adjacent corners that share a face. All three $\text{NH}_3$ are cis to each other at $90^{\circ}$. The opposite face is all three $\text{Cl}$. This is facial, fac.

Build the mer isomer**
Now arrange the three $\text{NH}_3$ so they wrap around the middle like a meridian: one up, one centre, one down in the same plane, so two $\text{NH}_3$ are trans ($180^{\circ}$ apart) and the third is cis to both. Fill the other three positions with $\text{Cl}$ in the same T shape. This is meridional, mer. Because the difference is cis versus trans positions in an octahedron, the type is geometric isomerism.

Final answer: fac-$\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_3\text{Cl}_3\text{]}$: three $\text{NH}_3$ on one face (each $\text{NH}_3$ cis to the other two), three $\text{Cl}$ on opposite face.
mer-$\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_3\text{Cl}_3\text{]}$: three $\text{NH}_3$ in a plane through Co (two trans to each other, one cis), three $\text{Cl}$ similarly in meridian.
Type: geometric (cis-trans) isomerism.

hints: Look at the structure of X and count the nitrogen atoms, then think about what each nitrogen owns that can be donated to a metal.
walkthrough:
Count donors, not atoms**
Look along $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. There are four N atoms, two $\text{-NH}_2$ ends and two $\text{-NH-}$ middles. Every N has one lone pair, so one molecule can donate four pairs, making four dative bonds. That is exactly what tetradentate means.
Final answer: Each of the four nitrogen atoms in X has a lone pair of electrons available to form a dative bond to the $\text{Co}^{2+}$ ion.

hints: Think of X as one ligand replacing several waters in a 1:1 reaction, balance the waters released to keep Co, charge and ligands conserved.
walkthrough:
Write the substitution**
One tetradentate X wraps around $\text{Co}^{2+}$ and kicks out water ligands: $$\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{18}\text{N}_4 \rightarrow \text{[Co(C}_6\text{H}_{18}\text{N}_4\text{)]}^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Charge stays $2+$. If X occupies only four sites, two waters can remain as $\text{[Co(C}_6\text{H}_{18}\text{N}_4\text{)(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$, which is also accepted.
